bibliographic.title: Beyond Expected Goals
bibliographic.venue: Proceedings of the 12th MIT Sloan Sports Analytics Conference

scope.rationale: Constructs a probabilistic physics-based pitch-control model that values game states (off-ball scoring opportunities, OBSO) from spatiotemporal tracking data, directly addressing action/state valuation in soccer.

model.name: Off-Ball Scoring Opportunity (OBSO)
inputs: spatiotemporal player tracking data (positions and velocities of all players at 25 Hz)
on-ball event data (match time, on-ball player, event type: pass, shot, goal, etc.)
model.target: Probability that the attacking team will score with the next on-ball event given the instantaneous game state (P(G|D))
model.architecture: Probabilistic physics-based model decomposed into three conditional components: (1) Potential Pitch Control Field (PPCF) modeling per-player control probability via a differential equation using time-to-intercept (logistic CDF) and ball time-of-flight with aerodynamic drag; (2) Transition model as a 2D normal distribution over next on-ball location scaled by PPCF^alpha; (3) Score model as a monotonic function of distance to goal raised to a power beta. Parameters fit via Bayesian MAP with normally distributed priors.
model.spatial_resolution: continuous (x,y) on the pitch, integrated as probability densities; PPCF computed per-player per-location

evaluation.splits: 5 games reserved as training set for parameter fitting; remaining 53 games used as test set. Split is at match level.

claims.statement: OBSO is more correlated with future goals than either shots or goals themselves are; per-player game-to-game PCC values are OBSO->OBSO 0.60, OBSO->shots 0.37, OBSO->goals 0.26, shots->shots 0.35, shots->goals 0.17, goals->goals 0.12.
The average goals/match versus average opportunity/match across the 14 teams in the 53-game test set has a Pearson correlation coefficient of 0.76.

MAP fits of the model parameters: s=0.54 sec (temporal uncertainty), lambda=3.99 Hz (control rate), kappa=1.72 (defensive advantage), sigma=23.9 m (transition spread), alpha=1.04 (PPCF exponent), beta=0.48 (score exponent).
The standard deviation of the average displacement between subsequent on-ball touches is 14 m.
For the example in Figure 5, the integrated magnitude of the OBSO is 1.1%.
In the example match between Team I and Team D with a final score of 1-1, integrated scoring opportunities are 1.32 versus 1.47 despite Team I dramatically outshooting Team D.
Player acceleration and maximum speed are modeled with fixed values of 7 m/s^2 and 5 m/s respectively for the time-to-intercept calculation.
The model assigns lambda_i = 0 to attacking players in an offside position, removing them from the control field.

The top 20 players ranked by mean OBSO/match are predominantly center forwards, but include a right winger, attacking midfielders, a center midfielder, a left winger, and notably a right back from Team A.

limitations: Score model ignores game state D apart from distance to goal; defensive positioning is only proxied through the PPCF rather than explicitly modeled in the score term.

Time-of-flight modeling choice (selecting the flight time that most closely matches the arrival time of the nearest attacking player) advantages successful passing to counteract limitations of the decision model.

The next on-ball event probability density lacks a preference for events that move the ball closer to the target goal, so opportunities that appear as clear scoring chances to a domain expert may be under-estimated.

The model does not directly account for the difficulty of crossing while running at speed, over-estimating chances in such scenarios and under-estimating chances for stationary, unpressured passers (footnote 7).
The opportunity for the player currently in possession is not considered in OBSO (footnote 8).
Small training set (5 games) and event-data synchronization issues motivate the Bayesian MAP approach with strong priors.
Event data timestamps carry stochastic noise on the order of three seconds, leading to moderate errors in player positions.
Future work is needed to refine the scoring model (Section 3.3) and the effect that defensive pressure and player speed have on the ability of a player to successfully deliver the ball to a teammate.
open_questions: Refine the scoring model to account for defensive pressure and player speed on pass completion.
Replace beta-based score adjustment with an improved scoring probability model in future iterations (footnote 6).
Incorporate a preference term for events that move the ball closer to the target goal in the transition density (footnote 5).
Allow per-player acceleration and maximum speed values to better model break-away situations (footnote 3).
Use the constituent control (PPCF) and transition models for additional soccer analyses beyond scoring.
